bottom_line: Prices are still rising too fast. US inflation hit 3.8%, and the Fed (the people who set interest rates) is almost certain to raise rates again, even after a rough week for stocks. That means borrowing money is about to get more expensive.

stories.title: Fed is getting ready to hike again
stories.real: Inflation rose in October, and the Fed's favorite price gauge hit a three-year high. Jobs numbers came in strong too. Traders now put the odds of a December rate hike at almost 100%, and reports say the Fed plans to go ahead despite the stock market turmoil.
stories.you: Credit cards, car loans and mortgages tend to cost more when rates go up, while savers can find CDs (locked savings accounts) paying up to 5.10%.

stories.title: Trump calls strong GDP number fake
stories.real: The government sharply raised its estimate of how fast the US economy grew last quarter (GDP, the total of everything the country produces), pointing to strong business investment and consumer spending. President Trump called the revision a mistake and 'fake' and demanded an investigation of the Commerce Department, the agency that puts out the number.
stories.you: A hot economy plus hot inflation is part of why the Fed is leaning toward raising rates instead of cutting them.

stories.title: AI stocks whipsaw, then bounce
stories.real: It was a bumpy, holiday-shortened week. AI stocks, especially Nvidia, swung hard after Jensen Huang's surprise return as CEO, and markets in Asia rode the same rollercoaster. AI stocks bounced back late in the week, and the Dow got back above 50,000 while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq struggled.
stories.you: If your retirement or index funds hold a lot of big tech, expect bigger swings, and single-stock ETFs (funds tied to just one company) swing even harder.

stories.title: New round of tariff threats
stories.real: The US plans fresh tariffs (taxes on imported goods) on 14 trading partners and is offering lower rates to countries that sign trade deals. Other countries have already rerouted some trade since the first round of tariffs.
stories.you: Tariffs can push up prices on imported goods, which gives the Fed another reason to keep rates higher for longer.

stories.title: Workers are feeling the squeeze
stories.real: The number of Amazon workers on food stamps has tripled, one example of workers getting a smaller share of the economy's money. In the UK, discount chain Poundland collapsed, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, and millions of homeowners face mortgage payments about £100 a month higher when their fixed deals end.
stories.you: A growing economy doesn't automatically mean bigger paychecks, so the high cost of everything is still biting regular households.
